Energy drinks in pregnancy: what the label can tell you

Updated: November 16, 2026

Written and edited by BeMama Authors team: checked against published guidance from recognized health organizations.

Halfway through a shift, you pick up a can labelled “energy”. Before opening it, check what the label means by one serving. Then look for the total caffeine and any herbal ingredients. A small can or a sugar-free claim tells you little about the amount of stimulant inside.

Count the whole container

Energy drinks can contain caffeine from added caffeine and ingredients such as guarana. A concentrated shot may be small but contain a substantial amount. If the label gives 80 mg per serving and the can holds two servings, the whole can provides 160 mg. If it lists caffeine per 100 mL, multiply by the number of 100 mL portions you drink.

The UK NHS advises no more than 200 mg of caffeine a day in pregnancy from all sources, including coffee, tea, cola and chocolate. Health Canada advises avoiding caffeinated energy drinks in pregnancy. Count any intake you have already had, but do not treat a daily caffeine limit as approval of a blend of stimulants.

What about the other ingredients?

Products vary. They may contain sugar or sweeteners, taurine, added vitamins or herbal extracts. Guarana contributes caffeine. Asian ginseng, also called Panax ginseng, has limited pregnancy safety data and some evidence of possible harm. Discuss any herbal product with your maternity clinician or pharmacist before taking it.

A long list of ingredients does not tell you that each one causes harm. It also does not demonstrate that a particular combination and dose are safe in pregnancy. For ordinary thirst or a break at work, choose water or another caffeine-free drink without added stimulants.

What research can tell us

A study drew on 7,304 pregnancies with information about energy drinks before pregnancy and 4,559 pregnancies with information on intake during pregnancy. Drinking them before pregnancy was associated with a higher risk of gestational hypertension. Few participants reported drinking them during pregnancy. The study could not establish that a drink caused high blood pressure or that a particular amount was safe.

If you already drank one

Save the label or take a photo. Note how much you drank, when, other sources of caffeine that day and how you feel. A single exposure cannot establish that the baby was harmed. If the amount is large or unclear, you used a concentrated product, or you feel unwell, contact your maternity team or local poison centre promptly for individual advice.

Call emergency services for chest pain, severe difficulty breathing, a seizure or collapse. If tiredness keeps interfering with work or daily life, mention it at your maternity visit so the team can consider causes and offer support.

Evidence-informed guidance

What trusted health organizations recommend

Check the caffeine in the whole container, including caffeine from guarana.

Use water or another caffeine-free choice for an ordinary drink.

Show the package to a clinician or poison centre after a concerning exposure.

How BeMama can help

BeMama suggests using the serving size and the number of servings on your own can to estimate what you drank before calling.

When to seek help

Seek prompt advice for a large or uncertain amount, concentrated caffeine or feeling unwell. Call emergency services for chest pain, severe breathing difficulty, a seizure or collapse.

Evidence notes updated: November 16, 2026

Key takeaways

  • Look for caffeine per serving, the number of servings, and herbal sources such as guarana.
  • Choose a caffeine-free alternative to an energy drink during pregnancy.
  • Keep the package and ask for advice if you consumed a large or uncertain amount or develop symptoms.

Frequently asked questions

Are energy drinks harmful during pregnancy?

Caffeinated energy drinks are discouraged because the amount of caffeine varies and the safety of added ingredients or combinations is uncertain. One drink does not prove harm to a pregnancy.

Why avoid them if I limit coffee?

Caffeine adds up across the whole day. A concentrated drink can contain several servings, and its other ingredients are a separate consideration.

Which ingredients should I look for?

Check the total caffeine, servings per container, guarana and other stimulants or extracts. Sugar-free does not mean caffeine-free. If the label is unclear, choose another drink.

Is ginseng suitable in pregnancy?

Asian ginseng has limited safety evidence in pregnancy and some findings raise concern. Avoid starting a ginseng supplement or a drink that contains it without advice from a maternity clinician or pharmacist.

This article is general education, not medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always talk with a qualified healthcare professional about your situation, and seek urgent care for emergencies.
